title: Princesses Don't Take the Bus
body:
I used to know my city. I was fluent in MUNI lines, fluent, I tell you; the kind of knowing that lives in the body rather than the brain–in knowing that I’d need to get on at the stop before Fillmore if I wanted a seat (because boy would that bus pack up real quick after), in that very particular agony of waiting at the first stop of each line, the bus sitting right there in front of you, going nowhere and making you wait (all while you’re grounded but went out anyway and have 30 minutes to get home before your parents do), and in the way you could be truly alone in a crowd and still feel full rather than empty. 

Do not mistake my use of past tense for displacement. I still live here: one and a half blocks from the 5 Fulton, technically two blocks from the 31 Balboa (if we are being generous about the length of my own block, which I think we ought to be), four to five blocks from the 38 Geary (the democratic thoroughfare that will carry you from the cold mouth of the ocean all the way to the gleaming teeth of downtown without so much as a single transfer), and 3-4 blocks from the 28 19th Ave bus. And if we are truly reaching, from Balboa to California Street, I live five blocks from the 1 California bus. Between these five lines I can get myself to virtually any corner of this city, or at the least, connect to something that will finish the job. You could say that I am, by any reasonable measure, extraordinarily well-served.

Within five minutes on foot is Golden Gate Park; the Music Concourse, the fountains, the de Young, the Academy of Sciences, the whole glorious impossible fact of it. My street has a bike lane running all the way down to the beach and within it, beginning at 25th Avenue, the slow streets begin (car-free, or close enough). JFK Drive, however, is now entirely car-free, which was controversial and generated op-eds and heated NextDoor threads, but which I loved with my entire heart. As did the Great Highway, Ocean Beach’s own boulevard, reclaimed from cars and returned to people and bicycles and the wind coming off of the Pacific.

I would bike through the trees on JFK, past the windmill at Beach Chalet, come out the other side, and there it would be: the ocean, glimmering and enormous. I would feel the wind on my face and think, with complete sincerity, how it was possible that the world could be so beautiful.

From this, it should be abundantly clear to you the richness of my circumstances. The fullness of my options. And the embarrassment, really, of my geographic wealth. Sure, a suburbia superfan may raise their eyebrows at this, and to them I say, respectfully, this essay is not for you. 

I should mention that for the record, I never got my driver’s license. I passed the age at which one typically gets a permit, and then the age at which one takes the test, and then several more ages after that, all without doing any of it. I know how to drive (and well at that, if I do say so myself), but the paperwork never seemed urgent. 

Then I went to Berkeley, where a car is obsolete, and so the question answered itself. 

When my boyfriend and I first started seeing each other, we would meet places I could easily reach, which was, as I have now extensively documented, everywhere. But to be specific, his neighborhood and mine, as well as the surrounding neighborhoods. This was truly less of a compromise and more of what I was capable of with what I had at my disposal.

But then we began dating properly, and I started sleeping over, so he would pick me up midday or at night and drive me to his, and then in the mornings he would drive me home. And I want you to understand that this was lovely. The city was still waking up, the fog not yet burned off, me in the passenger seat, half asleep and quite out of it. It felt like being taken care of and so I indulged myself. 

This is not a story about him. Nor am I suggesting that he was somehow the cause of what came after. The trap doesn't really need a villain in order to consume you. It doesn't need anyone to be cruel, or neglectful, or careless, or for someone to be haughty and think themselves above publicly funded transportation. It really just needs someone who loves you, and a system that is designed perfectly to take advantage of that love. The morning drives were, and still are, severely underappreciated by me. I don't want to pay for a Waymo or an Uber back. Taking the bus that early in the morning is beyond my comprehension. Walking is impossible. I could bike, but that would be even more fatiguing before I've even had coffee. At no point did any of this feel like a trade. It felt like nothing at all. It felt, simply, like a Tuesday morning in the city.

Here is something about me that you should know: I love people. They also exhaust me completely, so maybe I don’t always love people. This is not yet a contradiction that I have resolved. I’m simultaneously someone who craves company and someone who needs, desperately, to be alone. For a long time, the city solved this problem for me; I didn’t need to interact with anyone or need to perform or participate or make conversation over the noise of a restaurant playing music way too loud. Ultimately, I just needed to be among people; a body in motion among other bodies.

I still want that. I just can’t get myself to reach for it anymore.

What happened next happened gradually, and then all at once. Why take the bus (the bus I once knew like my own native tongue) when my boyfriend could just drive me? Why endure the indignity of an Uber, some stranger’s car smelling of someone else’s air freshener, forced small talk at a red light, when I could instead summon a Waymo and be entirely, gloriously alone? About this, however: I will take a car with no one in it over a car with a human in it every single time. I would rather be ferried around by a robot than make eye contact with a rideshare driver who I will sit in complete silence with for the entirety of the ride. At least the robot can’t comprehend awkward silence. 

But as most things do, even the robot has its terms. If the fare creeps past twenty five, thirty dollars, it is no longer worth it to me, and I simply do not go. Not I find another way. Not I take the bus instead. I just do. Not. Go. The bus, somehow, in the span of a few short years, became a place I could no longer locate myself going to. Biking became, in my mind, an act of needless self-punishment, when a robot could simply do the labor of moving my body through space while I sat there, useless and chauffeured, listening to my music through my Spotify account that automatically connects to the car’s system, scrolling endlessly on my phone.

I’m not sure I could call any of these decisions, exactly. Rather, they were the absence of decisions. A slow narrowing of what counted as an option, until the only ones left were: my boyfriend, or a robot under thirty dollars, or nothing at all.

Marx himself had a theory about what capitalism does to a person, and I’ve been thinking about it in relation to my own front door.

His argument, when stripped down to its bones, is this: under a hyper-capitalist logic, everything that makes you a full human being–the reading, thinking, theorizing, wandering, corresponding, it all gets quite discredited, treated as a waste of time. And when you stop doing those things, you lose the language for them. The vocabulary shrinks, the thoughts that needed those words become unthinkable. And eventually, you stop being a person who is things and become a person who has things. You trade your interior life for your accumulation. Your personality flattens into a single legible identity: a consumer, a worker, a passenger.

I am, I have recently realized, a passenger.

I don’t go anywhere anymore. I am taken places. I have traded the act of moving through my city, which was also the act of knowing it, reading it, being fluent in it, for the convenience of being delivered to it. The Waymo doesn’t know, nor does it care which stop comes before Fillmore and is the most optimal if you wanted a seat on the bus. Now, neither do I. The thoughts that needed those words, such as the wandering ones or the ones with no destination, are becoming harder to think.

I don’t attribute this to laziness or a personality flaw. I strongly believe that this is the exchange of being for having, arrived at my door in the form of a man I love and a robot car under thirty dollars.

But let us not make the mistake of thinking this is only about me.

The car did not only change how we move, it also redesigned the world to punish those who don’t have one. Suburbs built without sidewalks, strip malls surrounded by eight-lane parking lots so vast they constitute their own hostile geography, cities, and American cities, at that, and with great deliberation, that bulldozed entire neighborhoods, often ones with high demographics of often Black and brown neighborhoods, to make way for freeways that were never meant for the people who lived there. The built environment now physically encodes car-dependency, which means that the slow erosion of my transit instincts is a structural inevitability; the logical outcome of a world remade in the image of the automobile.

Well, what did the automobile remake, exactly? It killed the third place. Ray Oldenburg, who coined the term, meant the spaces between home and work where social life actually takes place; the bar, the park, the barbershop, the piazza, that corner that people gather at. Car-centric designs annihilated them. When everything requires driving to reach, you don’t get to wander into anywhere. You arrive at destinations, you do not linger, you do not stumble upon, and you do not run into anyone by accident. The serendipity of public space requires walkability, and walkability requires a world that isn’t organized around the car. Without third places, outside has no gravity. Without gravity, you stay in.

This here, is exactly the point. The car is the physical infrastructure of individualism; each person sealed in their own climate-controlled pod, insulated from the weather and the noise and the inconvenient presence of other people. Robert Putnam, in Bowling Alone, found that commute time was one of the strongest predictors of civic disengagement. Every ten minutes of driving: a measurable, documented decline in community participation. Every ten minutes. A society organized around the car is a society organized around the self and around the sealed-off and the delivered-to. It is essentially a society that, at the level of infrastructure, has decided other people are an inconvenience to be engineered around.

But the part that truly upsets me the most is that the dependency reshapes both behavior and your desire. This is what I find the most cruel.

It isn’t enough that the infrastructure is awful, that the third places are gone, that transit has been deliberately starved of funding to make the car seem inevitable by comparison, but the system also colonizes your wanting. You lose the ability to take the bus, sure, but you also lose the felt sense that the bus is an option. You stop being able to want to wander. The vocabulary shrinks, as Marx said, and I mean this with complete literalness, it shrinks until the thoughts that needed those words becomes unthinkable. I live one and a half blocks from the 5 Fulton. Obviously, I know this. But it now, on most days, feels unbelievably remote.

The car is sold to us as freedom or aspiration, or as the great American promise of going wherever you want whenever you want with whoever you want! But what it has actually produced is a two-tiered geography: those with car-access, and those without, left stranded in a world that is built for the former. But the inversion that goes unacknowledged: car-access itself, in a city like mine, becomes its own trap. The dependency it produces is its own kind of poverty of not being able to leave your house without someone else’s resources, someone else’s schedule, someone else’s willingness to drive you, and your proximity to that someone else. 

I shall be precise here about what I have lost, because I think precision matters exceptionally in this regard. In objective urbanist terms, I am richer than the rich. I have a massive park, I have five bus lines, I have a bike lane to the ocean and a car-free boulevard and windmills and the de Young and the fog and the glimmering, enormous Pacific, all within reach of my own two feet. By any measure that matters, I have everything.

And I have traded it for convenience.

This is the exchange you are neither warned about nor taught about. I have traded quality for convenience, independence for delivery, agency for the comfort of being taken care of, and my city for the passenger seat of someone else’s car.  And in doing so, I have forgotten, gradually and then completely, what it felt like to live. To experience the in-betweens, the inconvenient, the awfully frustrating, the bus that is running twelve minutes late, the hill you have to bike up before you get to coast down, the moment of waiting at the first stop, the bus sitting right there in front of you, going nowhere, making you wait. All of which I once knew, which I once catalogued as one of the textures of my life in this city.

A life of pure convenience removes hardship. And without hardship, how would you know a good thing if it were standing right in front of you? You wouldn’t. You don’t. Monotony ensues and everything flattens. The extraordinary becomes invisible because nothing is ever hard enough to make you notice it. I once felt the wind on my face at Ocean Beach and thought, with complete sincerity, how it was possible that the world could be so beautiful. I do not think that anymore. I am not sure, if I am being honest with you, that I think much of anything anymore, about beauty or the world or what it might feel like to move through it under my own power. 

I have forgotten what it is to have lived a good life. Not comfortable or convenient, but good.

So here I sit, possessed of every convenience in the world, shades drawn in my bedroom. I couldn’t tell you whether it’s sunny or gorgeous outside, whether the sky is blue or the fog has rolled in or the park is full of people living their lives without me. However, it’s summer, I’m sure it’s sunny. 

My boyfriend is driving back from Berkeley right now, and I will probably get picked up later so that we can hangout. I’ll consider asking him to stop at Green Apple Books on Clement (in fact I always consider it) but then get distracted by the far more alluring prospect of being chauffeured directly to his house and into his bed where I’ll sit there the exact same way I am now, the only difference being him by my side, pulling him directly into the same monotonous routine I’ve fallen into. A detour, after all, requires effort. Mental and physical effort. And as I have now exhaustively argued, that particular muscle has atrophied considerably.

Perhaps, upon writing this, I should take my own advice. Perhaps I shall go on a walk today. See JFK Drive. Stand in front of the de Young. Feel whatever the weather has decided to do with itself, whether it is raining and grey or unreasonably, offensively beautiful. My father has always called me a princess, on account of my deep and sincere affinity for the luxurious, the comfortable, the convenient. Princesses are rich in life, he means. And in this life, I’ve happened to entirely forget what actually makes me rich.

Maybe I’ll go on a walk and reassess that.

I’ve drawn open the shades. I was right; it is nice out today.

title: A Satisfied Person Is a Useless One
body:
Before we are old enough to consent–or even begin to comprehend life for that matter–we are arranged to desire in sanctioned directions. We come to these desires the way we come to our native tongue. It is fundamental to living at this point.

Institutions educate us, they provide us with worldly knowledge, with tools, with a sense of purpose and direction. Eventually, the direction becomes impossible to ignore. School is not preparing you for the world so much as it is preparing you for the next institution. Each student is carefully molded into someone who requires good grades to build a record, a record to appear desirable to universities, a degree to appear desirable to employers, and a career to work, dutifully and ceaselessly, until they have worked enough to stop being directed and begin directing others. That is, I suppose, the reward, as well as how you win.

But only a select few get to finish that journey. Most encounter blockades and hindrances along the way, erected by those who arrived before them; and these blockades do something perverse: it actually sharpens the hunger rather than discourages it. Competition ultimately feels like a law of nature. The top suddenly begins to matter less. Climbing is fatiguing. The top is still out of sight, but falling? Falling is out of the question. 

You want a simple life. You want your children to have a slightly better life than your lived simplicity, and you assume they’d likely want their children to also have a slightly better life than their lived simplicity, when the time comes. So, you bolster them up; you enroll them in the right schools, hire the right tutors, engineer the right experiences that are just diverse enough to appear as what could be considered as authentic selfhood; all in the service of making them desirable to the institutions that made you. 

The top continues to feel more daunting than it had before, and the dissatisfaction of never even getting a glance of it never resolves. You start to take notice: there are even more heights than before, more checkpoints, more distance from where you are and where you are supposed to want to be. This insatiable hunger is exactly the point. The motivating force doesn’t like you being satisfied, it enjoys the taunting. Because ultimately, a satisfied person is a useless one.

Until we have the capacity to locate this force within ourselves and refuse it, until we can find motivation that was not pre-installed, we will never be fully free. We will live simply, but precariously–always just afloat.

–

I have always been prone to intellectualization. It is both a liability and a gift: I can see the structure clearly, trace its architecture, name its mechanisms, tell you exactly how it was built, and redraw the blueprints upside down. And yet, I cannot exit it. My instincts, the ones we believe, and that I was told were my own, still desperately crave what the system asks me to crave. I feel the walls and care naught; I keep furnishing the room. 

As I’m sure most everyone wants, I do not want to be a slave to my labor. I want to follow my own passions and my own curiosity. But even my passions bear fingerprints that are not mine. The upholders of this system, its true believers–they are the ones who have shaped the landscape of what feels desirable. And here is the truly strange part: those individuals do not really exist either. Even at the top, the hunger will not resolve. The system is self-perpetuating, invisible, and entirely indifferent to you, and yet its imprint runs so deep that it essentially begins to feel like instinct. 

I know this, and I can see it. I still negotiate with it before I can do anything else. I can choose the work and life trajectory that feels truer to me, but I will choose to do it somewhere that guarantees I will not fall. That compromise, made entirely with open eyes, is its own kind of captivity.

This conflict, I cannot outgrow it. It becomes exponentially more complex, and not less, the older I get.

I tried climbing sideways for a while; a different direction, a different end goal, some exit that wasn’t the one everyone else was sprinting toward. But the top has a preposterously strong gravitational pull. It always appears closer than it is. I am not climbing toward it so much as I am tilting in its direction: diagonal and compromised, the run to its rise. I am moving, but really, I am not going where I said I would go.

And still I am incapable of pulling away. I know the strength of the magnetism, and I allow it to pull me. I walk directly alongside it. It visits me in dreams and offers false horizons, and I wake up lagging behind, reaching once again toward it. What do you call it when you despise something and cannot stop returning to it? When you are its most devoted critic, yet its most reliable participant? 

We have a toxic relationship, the system and I. I talk about it incessantly; at the dinner table, in the car, in essays, in the margins of my own life. I name it and call it what it is. And then I go back. I’m obsessed, I think.

I know the tower is watching, and I know the design of this place: the way that visibility itself becomes the mechanism of control, and the way you don’t need bars if the watched learn to watch themselves. I have read Foucault. I have nodded along. I am still inside the panopticon, behaving. I desperately need the guard to look away.

So what would it look like? If the guard was not looking my way, if I actually came upon the opportunity to run? 

I often try to picture it. A life ungoverned by the next credential or the next threshold and proof of desirability. Work that answers to nothing but itself. Days that do not accumulate toward any of the aspirations belonging to someone else. I try to hold the image and it dissolves. I have no reference for it. I have never seen it lived. I have read about it and romanticized it, maybe even fetishized it the way people fetishize things they cannot have. 

But really, the fantasy of escape was also given to me. The dream of the open road, the artist in voluntary poverty, the radical who renounced it all, the wannabe Thoreaus in search of their own Walden, unbeknownst to the fact that Thoreau was materially catered to the entire time. These are images the culture produced and distributed and made to feel transgressive while remaining entirely consumable. Even my vision of freedom has an aesthetic and my rebellion a mood board.

Maybe I am not imagining freedom at all. Maybe I am simply imagining a more palatable captivity. 

–

I used to aggressively criticize it, and people would, in turn, ask what the alternative was. I would subsequently feel utterly embarrassed that I didn’t know the answer. But now I think that not knowing is possibly the only honest answer anyone can give. My imagination does not exceed the boundaries of what I was given. But I know that it is not the same as it not existing. Nothing is impossible simply because it has not yet been modeled for us. And that is enough to keep me moving; the belief in something I cannot yet see.

Though I should be honest. Opting out requires resources. The freedom to choose any direction at all is itself a form of privilege. Exploration costs money. Defection costs stability. To break free, you must first give enough of yourself to it that you can afford to leave, which is, of course, its most elegant trap.

Maybe one day I will find the courage to freefall anyway, without a net, without a plan. I have no clue in the world how it will look. I’m not sure it will look like anything recognizable. But it happens in small acts of refusal; a deviation here, a compromise declined there, a slow accumulation of choices that are, incrementally, more mine. Until one day I can look back and realize that the footprints behind me are finally and unmistakably, my own.

title: Can you call yourself a leftist?
body:
My friends and I had a debate the other night about leftism as personal identity/lifestyle vs. leftism as collective political practice. I am someone who personally identifies as a leftist. However, it has become apparent to me that if you come from a background of privilege and eventually work a corporate job, it isn’t in your discretion to retain the title of a leftist. A true leftist would devote their life to their belief and cause. A true leftist would refuse to work for The Man in order to live in a commune. A true leftist wouldn’t sit around debating all day, they would go outside to advocate and work on legislation and policy! But a true leftist also wouldn’t work in policy because that is progressivism and liberalism, and not true leftism.

I claim all of this. I have been the person to work for The Man, I have debated political theory, and have sat around all day, sitting and agonizing with these thoughts. But I have also worked on policy that benefited working class San Franciscan residents. However, I am also someone who is financially stable and has endless support from my family and those around me. I will never know what it is like to struggle at the hands of capitalism and be at my wit’s end. I will never know what it is like to feel intense pressure to survive and build wealth in a world that is working against my attempts to do so. But ultimately, I maintain my stance and my belief. I claim the title of leftist.

If leftist, why not devote your life to leftism?

This is purity politics in its most essential form. Political belief does not require total lifestyle change. This argument is individualist and falls onto a liberal framework. Your personal career choices should not bear the burden of systemic change, that is the responsibility of our collective action. Leftism is not martyrdom. It should also not necessitate martyrdom. Limiting your options or purposely impoverishing yourself to relinquish all privilege in an effort to prove your sincerity ironically turns leftism into a movement accessible only by those who can afford to make that sacrifice. Arguing against leftist sincerity because one’s career isn’t their cause is confusing political identity with vocational identity.

The idea that you must be uncorrupted of capitalism in order to hold legitimate political views is a deeply individualist and almost Protestant notion that connotes salvation through personal virtue.

Structural privilege enables leftist belief.

This is true; I live within financial flexibility which allows me to indulge in these beliefs–the system itself will not completely destroy my livelihood. But, does this mean that only those without privilege can be authentic leftists? Should the people who come from stable families wait until they are financially independent in order to participate and engage politically? Isn’t that doing less, and not more?

Historically, the left has never actually been a movement of people that have fully exited capitalism. That is quite difficult to do, considering the current political and economic state of the world. In fact, navigating mainstream institutions while maintaining critical consciousness is closer to an organic intellectual (Gramsci) than vanguard purity politics.

Why not be someone that contributes something to the world then? Be a teacher or food bank worker!

Agree, those jobs are unbelievably admirable and generous. But if we really get into the technicalities, working at a food bank is structurally, a quite conservative act. The fundamental purpose of food banks is to patch the wounds that capitalism opened, while also not actually threatening the system that creates them. By making inequality more bearable, it also makes it more sustainable.

Teaching on the other hand: a very, very noble profession. But schools as institutions are, according to Gramsci and later by Althusser, ideological state apparatuses. In essence, they are mechanisms through which capitalist hegemony is passed on and transmitted to the next generation.

In fact, Althusser specifically argued in his essay Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses, that schools have replaced the church as the dominant ideological state apparatus under modern capitalism. Schools as institutions naturalize existing power relations and teach children to accept their place in the division of labor, effectively reproducing the conditions of capitalist production. Thus, if we go by this framework, teachers are functionally closer to priests of the existing order than to revolutionaries. This “teacher” argument is one that is ignorant to the most foundational leftist analyses of what teaching truly does structurally.

However, radical teachers do exist! Genuine leftist teaching appears more so as critical consciousness and challenging naturalized hierarchies. It’s teaching students to question before fully accepting. However, this specific practice is separate from the inherent function of the teaching profession.

We can continue on, and on, and on about all of these particular jobs that one could take over a capitalist or corporate career in order to be authentically leftist, but these jobs that people continuously bring up are based on aesthetic and cultural association. This argument is feelings-based rather than one of political conviction.

My point on working within capitalism.

In One Dimensional Man by Marcuse, he observed that advanced capitalism developed the ability to absorb opposition by turning it into a consumable aesthetic. Radical posturing, such as looking and performing radicalism, was one of the ways that the system neutralized genuine critique. Performing leftist authenticity through lifestyle choices is how capitalism defangs dissent by making it into an identity product.

Engels also, in Socialism: Utopian and Scientific, argued against the tendency to construct ideal communities and pure positions outside of existing society; for example, communes or separatist communities. This is what he called utopian socialism. According to him, this was sentimental and politically useless as it simply avoided the actual mechanisms of capitalist power rather than confronting it directly. A very good example of this is Henry David Thoreau’s Walden! His great experiment in radical self sufficiency was, the entire time, being subsidized by his mother doing his laundry and providing him with home-cooked meals, and land in the forest owned by Ralph Waldo Emerson, and provided free-of-charge for Thoreau.

However, these arguments force my hand at discrediting the work of food bank volunteers, teachers, and theorists who want to share their thoughts with the world.

Ultimately…

Leftism itself is a political consciousness and alignment. It should not be a lifestyle purity test or a constant need to prove your leftist sincerity. All jobs under capitalism are capitalist by definition, and this dissolves the moral hierarchy in which people construct between “good” and “bad” jobs. Critical consciousness, sustained belief, intellectual engagement, doing what you can with what you are able, are all legitimate and very meaningful forms of political practice. It is imperative that privilege be acknowledged in the flexibility of people following leftist ideology, as well as the inflexibility of those who must work tireless capitalist jobs for survival, but these acknowledgements should not be used to disqualify someone’s political alignment because privilege is a structural condition. We must be clear-eyed about difficulty and unbroken in commitment!

Many of my friends have nowadays succumbed to defeatism. But, I still believe that changing consciousness is still deeply valuable and matters significantly, even if I won’t live to see the outcome. Mark Fisher said that it is easier for us to imagine the end of the world before the end of capitalism. This pervasive atmosphere of inevitability is exactly what makes sustained belief feel naive and opposition feel futile.

However, if everyone internalizes capitalist realism and surrenders belief, then the self-fulfilling prophecy essentially fulfills itself. I strongly believe I will not see the end of capitalism. I think most, if not all, of the people around me would agree with this statement. But the difference is between those who give into defeatism, and those who hold open the possibility against the weight of everything trying to close it. This, here, is why I choose to retain my title of leftist.

title: Our Ascent into Techno-Feudalism
body:
“Once upon a time,” Marx and Engels wrote in The German Ideology, “a valiant fellow had the idea that men were drowned in water only because they were possessed with the idea of gravity. If they knock this notion out of their heads, say by stating it to be a superstition, a religious concept, they could be sublimely proof against any danger from water.” The man, they note, spent his entire mortal coil trying to cure humanity of this delusion, certain that by banishing the thought of gravity, he’d be able to abolish the fall itself. And his doctrine survives today in a new form.

Our widespread and general belief that material conditions can be overcome by the right idea now appears nearly everywhere: in billionaires who promise that we will reach emancipation and freedom from exploitative labor relations through software, in policymakers who outsource social crises to predictive models, in techno-spiritual evangelists who insist we are one update away from utopia, and even in everyday users who are convinced that their contradictions can be optimized away by better apps or products. The valiant fellow has simply multiplied; he now lives in each of us as we continue insisting that the ideal can override the material, that reality can be debugged if we just write the right line of code or use and implement the most efficient data structure. This is what Marx called ideology.

Marx provided us with an antidote for ideology: dialectics and historical materialism. He anticipated that material contradictions would eventually force capitalism to collapse in on itself. Instead, capitalism learned to reroute those contradictions, and what we are seeing now is capitalism with reorganized architecture: a change from industrial production to computational extraction. Surplus is now made with data and the owners of these oligarchical data and AI platforms occupy positions that seem to resemble feudal sovereignty far more than democratic enterprise.

Guy Debord’s Society of the Spectacle, Jean Baudrillard’s Simulation and Simulacra, and Michel Foucault’s Discipline and Punish, are of the utmost beneficence within this context. Taken together, this paper argues that these works provide the analytical tools through which we can understand how contemporary technological and AI systems reorganize agency, power, and knowledge in ways that allow capitalism to persist through mutation instead of collapse. In what I describe as our ascent into techno-feudal society, archaic, feudal structures return under the veneer of innovation, and positions owners of computational infrastructures as the new lords of digital territory, all while enclosing cognition and leaving users dependent and increasingly governed by systems they never get to see.

As written in The German Ideology, Marx and Engels believed that history advances through the tensions between material forces and our social relations. Time and again we have seen the coming and going of varying modes of production: primitive communal societies (egalitarian groupings and kinship-based organization), slave economies (ancient Greece and Rome), feudal lords (medieval Europe, parts of Asia, land-based economy), owners of capital (industrial revolution and onwards). Each of these carried a contradiction that would eventually result in its reshaping. However, for capitalism, the contradiction had been forecasted to be between labor and capital. As capitalist exploitation intensified, class consciousness would subsequently grow, and thus, the system would rupture, causing socialism to follow suit. But even through society’s current and supremely uncanny resemblance to what’s coined as “late-stage capitalism”, the end is far from near; the aforementioned linear transformation into communal living and shared resources appears as though it may never materialize. Instead, what we are seeing play out before us now, is capitalism avoiding its demise by absorbing the crisis into itself. Wage stagnation gave birth to debt markets, social discontent resulted in branding and lifestyle and identity politics. Each of these contradictions now presented an opportunity for reinvention.

Now, in 2025, we are seeing in full effect the forces of production abandon their industrial roots; they have become computational, and the primary supplier for surplus in this case, is data. This is our ascent into techno-feudalism.

A vocabulary is essential for understanding this transition. It helps to clarify and grasp what appears to be happening to reality and power. Debord, Baudrillard, and Foucault each offer conceptual tools that, albeit, when read together are fairly bleak, but are ultimately quintessential for thinking critically about what is to come. The theories do not all align and perfectly agree, but they fall along the same ideas, such as how agency is dissolving into simulation and how power is dissolving into infrastructures.

In Society of the Spectacle, Debord’s most largely heralded line claims that “the spectacle is not a collection of images, but a social relation among people, mediated by images” (Debord 4). Debord presents the spectacle as something that reorganizes the very structure of how we interact with and relate to everything and everyone around us, rather than as something we simply look at. Images stand between us and mediation becomes social relation. In this sense, the spectacle operates through representation; images reshape how individuals understand both themselves and others, while also subtly constraining the forms of agency available within that mediated world.

Social media’s intrinsic purpose was meant to strengthen connection and communication. Nowadays, users on social media produce content (“images”) as a currency; an attempt to embody signifiers of desire. Platforms encourage individuals to craft and piece together idealized versions of themselves that are calibrated to what others would want; yet the more that those signifiers are chased, the more disconnected we, the people, become from ourselves. What ends up getting lost here is agency understood as the capacity to define our own desires independently, as individuals become more and more susceptible to orienting their self-presentation around algorithmic feedback. This mirrors Todd McGowan’s Lacanian account of “ the desire of the Other” in his book Capitalism and Desire: “The capitalist subject constantly wonders which object is the [...] most desired by other subjects. [...] We desire what we assume the Other desires because the Other desires it and because we want to attract the desire of the Other.” This way, image replaces relationship.

Modern algorithms exacerbate this cyclic phenomenon: the more curated the image, the more feedback it generates; the more feedback it generates, the more it feels like desire; and the more it feels like desire, all the more we long to chase it.

TikTok’s For You Page, Instagram’s Explore tab and recommended Reels are but a few examples of how the spectacle is “the self portrait of power” (Debord 24). We see what power wants us to see; we relate through specifically curated feeds and branding scripts. Power owns the means of mediation, and mediation is now the structure of social existence.

But, this has been our reality for quite some time now, where images mediate our relations. The reality we are approaching, however, can be explained through Baudrillard’s Simulacra and Simulation. He details what happens when mediation actually goes beyond mediating, and replaces our reality altogether. Baudrillard writes that we now witness “the generation by models of a real without origin or reality: the hyperreal” (Baudrillard 1).

Baudrillard claims that simulation is “the substitution of the signs of the real for the real itself” (Baudrillard 2). Agentic AI (e.g., Perplexity’s Comet, OpenAI Agents mode) isn’t necessarily severing us from the world, we have our physical laptops in front of us, we use our fingers to type, scroll, click, receive. But, what changes with agentic AI is actually the level at which interaction occurs.

With agentic AI, we give up the autonomous acts of searching, comparing, reading, deciding, and calculating. In a Forbes article elaborating on Perplexity’s Comet browser, Steven Wolfe Pereira explains that “[agentic AI applications] complete complex, multistep tasks without constant human intervention” (Pereira). In place of our own selves, we allow the AI to perform those cognitive acts on our behalf. The device on which we prompt the AI remains tangible to us; the world remains accessible; yet our relation to it is now mediated by a model that interprets reality for us before we even get to encounter it. Even in earlier forms of digital life, interacting with technology still meant engaging with the full texture of information. We sorted through endless emails, carefully read through long articles and were able to recognize a distinct and authentic voice, booked flights with lots of frustration and deliberation, and added items to our calendar because we wanted to remember them. Though these interactions were not necessarily “authentic” in a typically romantic sense, they required attention to detail, patience, as well as interpretation. In order to perform these acts, we were made to move through the world with some friction, and that friction is exactly what contributes to defining and creating meaning. It reflects a process of co-production; meaning and subjectivity emerge through sustained interaction between people and technologies rather than being instantaneously delivered.

Agentic AI removes all of these micro-encounters; it compresses writing and extracts structure. Ultimately, we are presented with the “essence” without an understanding of the time or interiority that created it. The model is the first encounter, and we become spectators of the agent’s engagement, all while removing ourselves as participants in our own.

Nevertheless, in a world where productivity is a condition of survival, it’s understandable that people may wish for tools that can streamline tedious tasks. When labor markets punish patience and the slowness of process, or when academic environments reward perceived merit and consistent output, automation offers a breather. And wanting that kind of relief is not to be mistaken as, or interpreted as moral failure. It should be seen as a structural failure.

The danger here is the slope of automation’s trajectory; automating what’s tedious, to automating the interpretive, to automating the relational, and finally to automating the self.

Many engagements benefit from offloading and streamlining. But others, such as reading or thinking, lose so much of their fundamentality when a model performs it for us. It ultimately prevents us from being able to see the world with our own eyes before the simulation ends up handing its conclusion down to us.

Agentic AI interposes an optimized version of the world that steadily and gradually becomes the only version we engage with.

We turn to Foucault to see how power runs underneath all of this. According to Foucault in Discipline and Punish, power is diffused through institutions, and exercised through practices of classification and surveillance. Knowledge allows us to arrange the world so that certain actions or behaviors can be governed.

Another dimension of techno-feudal power can be seen in the growing dependence on AI as an intermediary for knowledge itself. Students are encountering information through AI platforms that are able to summarize and reorganize material on behalf of textbooks or teachers at an exponential rate. In Discipline and Punish, Foucault describes the concept of “docile bodies”. He writes, “A body is docile that may be subjected, used, transformed, and improved” (Foucault 136). The contemporary student is now shaped by interfaces that streamline thinking and agency to perform interpretive labor to the point where intellectual work becomes almost entirely indistinguishable from compliance. Efficiency can be interpreted as neutral or even benevolent, but it ultimately produces what Foucault would call a docile epistemic subject; something that is predictable and easily guided.

When AI outputs appear authoritative and credible, the user never really sees the exclusions that structure them. Foucault claims that “power and knowledge directly imply one another” (Foucault 27), essentially meaning that whoever gets to control or own the production of knowledge also controls the formation of subjects, which is why the increasing reliance on AI is dangerous. A model update can alter political assumptions or change what counts as credible evidence, all while these changes remain unbeknownst to the public.

Another of Foucault’s central insights: “the individual is not to be conceived as a sort of elementary nucleus [...] it is one of the prime effects of power” (Foucault 29). As students turn to AI summaries and syntheses, their habits of thought start to match the exact structures that the system provides. The subject that thus emerges is one that is molded through convenience; someone that learns to think in the formats that AI makes easiest to access.

When the production of knowledge becomes automated, the production of judgment follows closely behind. In a system ruled by techno-feudal power, the same platforms that mediate the truth also get to determine where each person stands within the hierarchy they create. Foucault writes, “the examination [...] established over individuals a visibility through which one differentiates and judges them” (Foucault 184).

In education, AI graders and plagiarism detectors transform assignments into streams of data. Students get parsed as patterns or anomalies, rather than being truly evaluated as a thinker, or for the value of their work. Each submission would theoretically add another data point that situates them within categories that the system itself created. This exact same process governs workplaces using systems like keystroke monitors or productivity dashboards. And because this examination enforces and produces the subject that it judges, individuals internalize these categories long before any actual explicit evaluation gets to occur. The process is essentially performative; people pre-optimize their behavior and learn to match the preferences of the system that classifies them. They are hence shaped by the visibility that surrounds them, and AI platform owners get to define the terrain of knowledge and the terms by which subjects navigate it.

However, the theories only matter insofar as they touch the ground. The ascent into techno-feudalism creeps its way into various nooks and crannies, with each small shift revealing just how much power has begun to consolidate behind all of the systems we’ve come to consider as neutral.

Palantir renders this movement concrete. It presents itself as a neutral data processor, claiming to produce “products for human-driven analysis of real-world data” (Palantir), all the while its platforms modify entire categories of knowledge. Palantir’s own systems have been enlisted by the United States government and outsourced to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for “workplace raids, large-scale enforcement operations, and investigations involving asylum seekers—showing how Palantir’s pattern-finding capabilities have long been central to ICE’s most aggressive tactics” (Hubbard). Palantir outrightly produces classifications such as “risk,” “threat,” or “suspicious activity” and these classifications become a mechanism of power, they act as the lenses that authorities see through to police citizens; governance through anticipation. People behave very differently when they know every movement or association is logged somewhere, and is fed into a model that they never actually get to see. What emerges is a form of authority that feels atmospheric and inconspicuous rather than direct. This is power that operates in the way that Foucault warned modern institutions would operate; by scaffolding what you might do before you even get to do it.

This same logic applies to San Francisco’s newest private K-8 institution, Alpha School. Alpha School markets itself as a place where academic tasks are handled in just two hours a day by AI so that students can spend the rest of their time learning life skills and participating in creative activities like designing or owning a food truck (Buller). There is intuitive appeal here; digital literacy is undeniably essential now, more than ever, in our world where information is provided through interfaces rather than books, and having the ability to navigate technological and computational systems will become imperative as our society becomes more and more datafied.

But for young and highly impressionable children who are just beginning to develop cognition, having their first exposure to knowledge be mediated through an AI system that summarizes and curates for you risks turning learning into another form of software assistance. Children who never get to struggle through a textbook or article unaided or never experience confusion that only personal effort resolves, will develop a worldview in which insight is believed to be something that is simply fetched and not built. This is not to be interpreted as a hysterical objection to technology however; children should learn to interact with AI. But before learning how to delegate thinking, children should first and foremost learn how to think for themselves. Otherwise, the owners of AI will go beyond building educational software and begin to formulate the conditions through which learning is experienced. Digital literacy without intellectual literacy does nothing for the greater good of society if it only produces subjects who know how to use tools but not how to resist them.

When the map precedes the territory long enough, people start to mistake the map for the world.

Through historical materialism, Marx assumed that we would arrive at resolution through rupture. But capitalism had a different idea; it discovered recursion by learning from its own failures and finding new domains from which to extract value, foreboding our ascent into techno-feudalism.

The danger of this is how cognition itself is becoming enclosed. Ultimately, when all interpretation and judgment are delegated into opaque infrastructures, our autonomy unwittingly erodes right before our eyes. This requires all of convenience and asymmetry of ownership, and none of conspiracy.

In an effort to mitigate this trajectory, we must insist on cognitive literacy before delegation and public accountability over privately governed infrastructures. Education must teach how systems work before we allow or ask students to rely on them, and platforms that mediate reality must be subject to democratic scrutiny, rather than treated as tools that are neutral for all. Autonomy and human agency are cultivated; if they are not actively protected, they’ll eventually be optimized away.

Digital infrastructures are not inherently corrosive. But who owns the means of cognition and who controls the frames through which truth is filtered must be accounted for and held responsible. Otherwise we put ourselves at risk of recreating the valiant fellow’s delusion; believing that by creating systems and interfaces that are more and more efficient we can abolish gravity. But the fall remains, it just now happens inside systems that insist it is flight.

title: Dear Paris,
body:
May 13, 2026

“In the beginning I was so young and such a stranger to myself I hardly existed. I had to go out into the world and see it and hear it and react to it, before I knew at all who I was, what I was, what I wanted to be.” - Mary Oliver, Upstream

“No amount of security is worth the suffering of a mediocre life chained to a routine that has killed your dreams.” - Maya Mendoza

“If adventures will not befall a young lady in her own village, she must seek them abroad.” - Jane Austen, Northanger Abbey

I left San Francisco on January 13th, and arrived in Paris on January 14th, 2026. It has officially been 5 months since my departure, and in 2 days, I must pack my bags, empty this entire apartment, and hail a cab to Charles de Gaulle airport, where I will head back to San Francisco, my home.

But why is it that the term “home” has never felt less fitting for a city in which I had spent 90% of my life in? Where my family resides, my college town that is but a 40 minute car ride away, and where friends who I have known for years on end all coexist in the same 7 by 7 mile radius? A massive and growing knot has made itself known within the depths of my stomach, and I can’t help but acknowledge it, as much as I wish that I could pretend not to know of its existence. It is twisting and turning, and feels like a deadweight. I feel lightheaded from the overwhelming and unbearable nature of it. I wish to take a shovel and scrape it out from within. Because it is always easier to dissemble that you are not emotionally affected by things outside of your control than it is to face it head on and attempt to defeat it by your own resourcefulness and willpower. I know very, very well what the catalyst for this knot’s rapid development is. However, accepting it is another issue. 

I recently found out that Paris is around 15% smaller than that of San Francisco. I truly thought to myself, that this was impossible and someone must be calculating wrong, or measuring wrong. The city I had to come to know as one of the smallest, most suffocating cities in the world is bigger than the city in which I was able to realize and invest in my true desires and passions? Endless opportunities and surprises materialized around each corner in Paris; I was never lacking in wonder and glory, inspiration continued to find me time and time again, even on the nights in which I felt too depressed to rise from my bed. I can’t quite articulate what exactly the difference-maker in this situation was, and I am well aware of the fact that revelations as such are not directly caused by location and are entirely derived from within, but it has become supremely arduous not to associate experiences with where they took place. Don DeLillo painted it quite well: “That’s why people take vacations. Not to relax or find excitement or see new places. To escape the death that exists in routine things.” But is it bad of me to claim this not as vacation, considering I lived here for an extended period of time? Am I allowed? For the sake of this essay, letter, dedication, I will proceed with this belief.

I believe that San Francisco, in all of its beauty and distinctiveness, causes me to feel emotionally and experientially stunted because of what ties me to that city. The reputation I uphold, the versions of myself that have come and gone yet still persist in peoples’ minds, the expectations that befall me in a place that knows my hopes and dreams, the people who expect particular achievements from me; it’s all just so stifling. I feel smothered and strangled. I am fully incapable of separating these instances from the city itself, and it is truly such a shame, as San Francisco is my beloved home and safe haven. Its dichotomous nature is a nightmare and I wish I had the mental power to erase all of the aversions I’ve accumulated over the years.

I do not particularly like the identity I upkeep at home. It isn’t what I feel genuinely reflects my truest form, and while it is entirely within my control to align my identity, it feels impossible to do so in a place where I have come to feel the most comfortable as that version of myself. I don’t know anything outside of the person I am at home, when at home. But uprooting my entire life and running across the world to remain here in Paris, permanently, feels incredibly daunting. I hate to admit it, but I do tend to feel the most comfortable in a familiar space. Perhaps I just need to familiarize myself even more so with Paris. Or maybe I am just afraid that I may grow to resent this new version of myself as well and that it is better off being left as an amazing, yet melancholic memory.

Here’s to her, the me who I have truly loved and adored over these several months. I shall dedicate a toast to her, and to the place that made her:

Paris has never freed someone more desperate to escape the shackles they imposed on themselves. She arrived uncertain, and left - or is leaving - with something harder to name nad more ambiguous than confidence. The time she spent at Parsons Paris will especially be cherished, and those who have made an imprint on her, will be cherished above all. Parsons gave her a room full of people who didn’t know any prior version of her, and she was ultimately surprised to find that without the weight of everyone else’s memory, she could finally hear herself think. Even the rain that persevered despite everyone’s’ wishes for sunlight, could not dampen the memories and experiences she (May 21st 2026 cont.) now holds in her heart forever.

- -

The other day, my friend said to me, that another friend had said to her, “Wherever I go, there I am.” It sounds ridiculously pseudo-intellectual, of that I am fully aware, in fact I had a hearty chuckle upon hearing that, but it also cut deep in a way nothing else really had. I’ve spent my entire life running away from cities and countries in search of new and uncharted territory, a place where no one knew who I was, somewhere I could be whomever and whatever I wished to be, and free from the expectations people held of a previous version of myself. Each time I found a new and sufficient setting, I felt like a bird, free from societal structures, with only an empty and vast blue sky that stretched endlessly before me, unbound from any single path or route. I could shed who I was and assume a new form.

But what a miserable life to lead. I don’t want to get up and move across the world each time I get tired of myself and the way people perceive me. I need to learn how to grow and make change without running away. And Paris had in fact, helped me learn just a little, how I should approach doing so. 

Thus, I hope that going forward, rather than revert to this constant and revolting inclination to escape or grow endlessly restless with myself, I will try something harder and learn to tolerate myself and my situation, “[because] it’s inside myself that I must create someone who will understand.” - Clarice Lispector.

Thank you, Paris. This won’t be the last you see of me!
